with the [[Miami Dolphins]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]], earning first-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1981. Marino was the last quarterback taken in the first round of the famed [[1983 NFL draft|quarterback class of 1983]]. |website=Audacy |language=en}} Best remembered for his quick release and powerful arm, Marino helped the Dolphins become consistent postseason contenders, leading them to the playoffs ten times and one Super Bowl appearance in [[Super Bowl XIX|XIX]], although a title victory ultimately eluded him during his career. Marino is considered by many to be one of the greatest players to never win a Super Bowl{{cite web|url=http://www.sportsonearth.com/article/252946756/best-nfl-active-retired-players-without-a-ring|title=Best active and retired NFL players without a Super Bowl ring|last=Arthur|first=Kenneth|work=sportsonearth.com|publisher=MLB Advanced Media, LP|date=September 7, 2017|access-date=January 10, 2019|archive-date=March 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190314012751/http://www.sportsonearth.com/article/252946756/best-nfl-active-retired-players-without-a-ring|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=https://www.foxsports.com/nfl/story/20-best-players-to-never-win-a-super-bowl-020317|title=20 Best Players to Never Win a Super Bowl|last=Pollin|first=Tom|date=June 30, 2017|work=foxsports.com|publisher=Fox Sports Interactive Media, LLC|access-date=January 10, 2019}}{{Cite web|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1025782-50-greatest-quarterbacks-never-to-win-a-super-bowl|title=50 Greatest Quarterbacks Never to Win a Super Bowl|first=Tony|last=Santorsa|website=Bleacher Report}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/the-best-quarterbacks-to-never-win-a-super-bowl-2012-1|title=The Best Quarterbacks To Never Win A Super Bowl|first=Cork|last=Gaines|website=Business Insider}} and has the most career victories of quarterbacks not to win a title at 155. A nine-time Pro Bowl selection, eight-time first (3) or second (5) team [[All-Pro]],{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MariDa00.htm |title=Dan Marino |website=pro-football-reference.com |access-date=2026-03-06}} and All-AFC six times, Marino was voted [[National Football League Rookie of the Year|NFL Rookie of the Year]] by ''[[Sporting News]]''. The following season in 1984, Marino was the [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|NFL Most Valuable Player]] (MVP) and Offensive Player of the Year, when he set single-season records of 5,084 passing yards, 48 touchdown passes, nine 300-yard passing games, and four 400-yard passing games. He was voted the 1994 [[NFL Comeback Player of the Year]], and the 1998 [[Walter Payton Man of the Year Award|NFL Walter Payton Man of the Year]]. Marino threw the most TD passes of the entire decade of the 1980s (220) despite only playing in 7 seasons of the decade (1983–89); and threw for the most passing yards in the entire decade of the 1990s (33,508). Marino is the only quarterback in NFL history to lead in either category in back-to-back decades, and the lone one to lead the league in all three passing categories of completions, passing yards, and touchdown passes for three consecutive years (1984–1986). At the time of his retirement, Marino held more than 40 NFL single-season and career passing records (many of which have since been surpassed), including career passing attempts (8,358), completions (4,967), passing yards (61,361), and touchdown passes (420). His career [[passer rating]] of 86.4 was the fourth-highest in NFL history (fifth when including stats from the [[All-America Football Conference|AAFC]]).{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/pass_rating_career_1999.htm | title=NFL Career Passer Rating Leaders Through 1999 | website=pro-football-reference.com | access-date=June 30, 2025}} Marino was the first quarterback in NFL history to reach [[List of NFL quarterbacks with 5,000 passing yards in a season|5,000 yards passing in a season]] (1984); 50,000 and 60,000 career passing yards respectively, and also the first quarterback to reach 40-plus touchdown passes in a season (48 in 1984), and 400 career touchdown passes. Marino was enshrined into the [[Miami Dolphins Honor Roll]] immediately after his retirement in 2000, inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2003, inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2005 in his first year of eligibility, and is currently one of only three former Miami Dolphins to have his jersey number retired. In 2019, Marino was named to the [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]] as one of the 10 greatest quarterbacks in NFL history, as determined by a panel of coaches and media members.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/100/all-time-team/roster|title=NFL 100|website=NFL.com}} ==Early life== Born and raised in [[Pittsburgh]], Pennsylvania, Marino is of [[Italian Americans|Italian]] and [[Polish Americans|Polish]] ancestry. The oldest child of Daniel and Veronica (Kolczynski) Marino, he has two younger sisters, Cindi and Debbie.{{Cite web|title=Marino, Daniel Constantine, Jr. ("Dan") – Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives, Thematic Series: Sports Figures |url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G2-3436500390.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131105214725/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G2-3436500390.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=November 5, 2013|date=November 5, 2013|via=[[HighBeam Research]] |url-access=subscription |work=Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives, Thematic Series: Sports Figures |access-date=May 9, 2020}} His father delivered newspapers for the ''[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]'',{{cite web |author=Powell, Albrecht |url=http://pittsburgh.about.com/od/famous_locals/p/dan_marino.htm |title=About.com Guide |access-date=May 5, 2010 |archive-date=January 13, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080113161108/http://pittsburgh.about.com/od/famous_locals/p/dan_marino.htm |url-status=dead }} and Marino grew up on Parkview Avenue in the [[Oakland (Pittsburgh)|South Oakland]] neighborhood.{{cite web |author=Grupp, John |url=http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/s_300851.html |title=Marino has come a long way from Parkview Avenue |work=[[Pittsburgh Tribune-Review]] |date=February 6, 2005 |access-date=May 5, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100303205053/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/s_300851.html |archive-date=March 3, 2010 }} He attended St. Regis Catholic Elementary School and graduated from [[Central Catholic High School (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)|Central Catholic High School]] in 1979, where he starred in [[baseball]] for the Vikings and won ''[[Parade magazine|Parade]]'' [[All-America#High school sports|All-American]] honors in [[High school football|football]]. In the [[1979 Major League Baseball draft]], Marino was selected in the fourth round by the [[1979 Kansas City Royals season|Kansas City Royals]],{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=y4JIAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ym0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=7007%2C3079904 |work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |last=Hecht |first=Steve |title=Pitt hurls wrench in Marino's talks with Kansas City |date=June 23, 1979 |page=10}} but decided to play college football instead.{{cite news|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1009455/2/index.htm |work=CNN |title=Video |date=February 17, 1997 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100509042849/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1009455/2/index.htm |archive-date=May 9, 2010 }} ==College career== [[File:MarinoColorPitt1979.jpg|thumb|left|267px|[[Pittsburgh Panthers football|University of Pittsburgh]] freshman (1979)]] Marino attended the [[University of Pittsburgh]], and played for the university's [[Pittsburgh Panthers football]] team from 1979 to 1982. As a freshman in [[1979 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1979]], Marino led the Panthers in a 24–17 triumph over [[West Virginia University|West Virginia]] in the [[Backyard Brawl]] and a 29–14 win over longtime rival [[Penn State Nittany Lions|Penn State]]. Pitt's [[1980 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1980 Marino-led team]] finished No. 2 in the season-ending rankings (''[[The New York Times]]'' computer poll rated Pitt as No. 1). Marino was part of an elite team during those two years that included two other future NFL Hall of Fame players: Defensive lineman [[Rickey Jackson]] and center [[Russ Grimm]], as well as future Pro Bowl linebacker [[Hugh Green (American football)|Hugh Green]] and future Pro Bowl guard [[Mark May]]. In 1980, Pitt added future NFL players [[Bill Maas]], [[Dwight Collins]], and [[Tim Lewis]], while their offensive line got a third future Pro Bowl player: tackle [[Jimbo Covert]]. "There were games when my uniform never got dirty," Marino once remarked. "There were games when I never hit the ground. That's incredible."{{cite web | title=College Days: Russ Grimm | website=Pro Football Hall of Fame|date=October 3, 2013| url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2013/10/news-college-days-russ-grimm/ | access-date=2025-09-03}} Following the [[1981 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1981 regular season]], Marino led the Panthers, who had been ranked No. 1 most of the season, to a last-minute triumph over the No. 2 [[1981 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia Bulldogs]] in the [[1982 Sugar Bowl]] by throwing a game-winning pass to tight end John Brown with less than a minute remaining in the game. Marino later cited this as the most memorable pass he'd thrown in his college career.{{cite magazine|title=Face to Face with Dan Marino |magazine=[[Electronic Gaming Monthly]]|issue=86 |publisher=[[Ziff Davis]]|date=September 1996|page=134}} He led the nation with 34 passing touchdowns.{{Cite web |title=1981 College Football Leaders |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/years/1981-leaders.html |access-date=November 20, 2025 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}} Overall, during the three seasons from 1979 through 1981, Pitt garnered 33 wins with only 3 losses (three straight 11–1 seasons) and was constantly ranked in the top 5 of both major media polls. The Pitt football team's fortunes and Marino's statistics dipped during [[1982 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|his senior year]], which saw the team transition from head coach [[Jackie Sherrill]] to new coach [[Foge Fazio]], culminating in a 7–3 loss in the 1983 [[Cotton Bowl Classic]] to [[Southern Methodist University]] and their "Pony Express" of [[Eric Dickerson]] and [[Craig James (running back)|Craig James]]. Marino finished ninth in voting for the [[Heisman Trophy]] in 1982, after finishing fourth the previous year.{{cite news |author=Baker, Chris |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=January 5, 1983 |page=D3 |title=... And Now to the No. 1 Task of Signing Marino: Express Make Pitt Quarterback Top Selection; UCLA's Ramsey Is Also on L.A. List}} Marino finished his four college seasons with 8,597 passing yards, 79 touchdowns, and 69 interceptions.{{cite web |title=Dan Marino CFB Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/dan-marino-1.html |publisher=[[Sports Reference|Sports Reference LLC]] |work=Sports-reference.com |access-date=February 14, 2021 |archive-date=November 12, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112020134/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/dan-marino-1.html |url-status=dead }} ==Professional career== ===NFL draft=== Marino's selection status in the [[1983 NFL draft]] plummeted after his weaker senior season at Pitt{{r|30for30}} and rumors of [[recreational drug use]].{{cite web |author=Schultz, Jeff |url=http://blogs.ajc.com/jeff-schultz-blog/2010/04/19/dwyer-will-overcome-bad-pre-draft-rumor/ |title=Jonathan Dwyer will overcome bad pre-draft rumor | Jeff Schultz |publisher=Blogs.ajc.com |date=April 19, 2010 |access-date=September 28, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100716124438/http://blogs.ajc.com/jeff-schultz-blog/2010/04/19/dwyer-will-overcome-bad-pre-draft-rumor/ |archive-date=July 16, 2010 }} Five other quarterbacks—[[Ken O'Brien]], [[Tony Eason]], [[Todd Blackledge]], and Hall of Famers [[Jim Kelly]] and [[John Elway]]—were drafted ahead of him in the first round. [[Bill Hillgrove]], who was with the Marino family on draft day, later recalled that when the [[New York Jets]] selected O'Brien, Marino "became visibly ill". (O'Brien, who played for [[NCAA Division II|Division II]] [[UC Davis Aggies football|Cal-Davis]], was so obscure that Marino later asked his agent Marvin Demoff "Who is Ken O'Brien?"){{r|30for30}} The [[Miami Dolphins]] chose Marino as the 27th pick in the first round. He did not expect to be available for the team to draft, so he never spoke to head coach [[Don Shula]] or anyone else from the Dolphins before the coach called after the selection.{{Cite web |last=Florio |first=Mike |author-link=Mike Florio |date=May 5, 2020 |title=Dan Marino didn't meet Don Shula before being drafted by Dolphins |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/dan-marino-didnt-meet-don-shula-before-being-drafted-by-dolphins |access-date=May 6, 2020 |website=ProFootballTalk |language=en-US}} Opinion was divided on the wisdom of the team's decision; [[Chris Berman]] said that Shula was "the best", but [[Paul Lionel Zimmerman|Paul Zimmerman]] was skeptical of the coaching staff's ability to help Marino "overcome the problems he's had". Shula later said that being passed up by so many teams "motivated [Marino] to show everybody else what a mistake that they had made".{{cite episode | title=Elway to Marino | series=30 for 30 | network=ESPN | airdate=April 23, 2013 | season=2}} ===Early years and Super Bowl appearance=== Marino was the first draft pick in the history of the [[United States Football League]], selected by the [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|Los Angeles Express]]. He did not sign with the team, choosing instead to sign with the Dolphins. After starting the season as a backup to incumbent starter [[David Woodley]], Marino was given his first NFL start in week 6 versus the [[Buffalo Bills]]. Marino and Miami lost that game 38–35 in overtime. As a rookie, Marino set several records: he posted a 96.0 passer rating, he was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] as a rookie, he had the lowest percentage of passes intercepted with 2.03, he was the only rookie quarterback to lead a conference in passing, and he had the highest passing completion percentage with 58.45. Marino was The Sporting News Rookie of the Year and was also named 2nd Team AP [[All-Pro]]; the first and still only rookie QB to be named All-Pro in the Super Bowl era.{{cite web |url=http://www.dolphinsinfo.com/marinop.htm | title=Dan Marino Page |access-date=December 21, 2011}} The Dolphins finished the season with a 12–4 record and advanced to the AFC divisional playoffs, where Marino threw two touchdown passes in his playoff debut. However, he also threw two interceptions as the team lost to the 9–7 [[Seattle Seahawks]], 27–20.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198312310mia.htm |title=Divisional Round – Seattle Seahawks at Miami Dolphins – December 31st, 1983 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=February 28, 2018}} In his second season, Marino broke six NFL full-season passing records, including the records for most touchdown passes (48, surpassed by [[Peyton Manning]] in 2004) and most passing yards (5,084, surpassed by [[Drew Brees]] in 2011), and was selected as the NFL's [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|Most Valuable Player]]. He was also voted 1984 Offensive Player of the Year, and 1st Team AP All-Pro. Marino led the league in completions, yards, and TD passes and the Dolphins finished with a 14–2 regular-season record, clinching home-field advantage for the playoffs. In the Divisional round, the Dolphins avenged their playoff loss of the previous season to the [[Seattle Seahawks]] 31–10 behind Marino's 262 passing yards and 3 touchdowns.{{cite web|title=Dan Marino: Biography|url=http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/member.aspx?PLAYER_ID=238|publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame|access-date=February 10, 2015|archive-date=August 6, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110806005648/http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/member.aspx?player_id=238|url-status=dead}}{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198412290mia.htm |title=Divisional Round – Seattle Seahawks at Miami Dolphins – December 29th, 1984 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=February 28, 2018}} The next week the Dolphins defeated the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the AFC Championship Game 45–28.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198501060mia.htm |title=AFC Championship – Pittsburgh Steelers at Miami Dolphins – January 6th, 1985 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=February 28, 2018}} In that game, Marino set AFC Championship Game records with 421 passing yards and 4 touchdowns, despite throwing his last pass of the game with 11:07 still remaining on the clock. Both records still stand as of 2026. [[File:Marino HOF jersey.jpg|thumb|270px|Marino's jersey shown at the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in Canton, Ohio]] In [[Super Bowl XIX]], Marino and the Dolphins faced off against the [[1984 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]] and [[Joe Montana]] in [[Palo Alto, California]]. The Dolphins, who had 74 rushing attempts in the previous two weeks, ran the ball only eight times in this game. Marino finished with 29 completions out of 50 attempts for 318 yards, throwing one touchdown pass and two interceptions (both late in the game with the score already decided). The Dolphins lost 38–16 in what was Marino's only Super Bowl appearance.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198501200mia.htm |title=Super Bowl XIX – San Francisco 49ers vs. Miami Dolphins – January 20th, 1985 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=February 28, 2018}} In 1985, Marino threw for 4,137 yards and 30 touchdowns while leading the Dolphins to the AFC Championship game.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/1985.htm|title=1985 Miami Dolphins|publisher=pro-football-reference.com|access-date=February 10, 2015}} On September 29, Marino threw for 390 yards and 3 touchdowns in the Dolphins' 30–26 victory over the [[1985 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]], in the first matchup between Marino and Broncos quarterback [[John Elway]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198509290den.htm |title=Miami Dolphins at Denver Broncos – September 29th, 1985 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=February 28, 2018}} Then on December 2, Marino threw for 270 yards and 3 touchdowns against the [[1985 Chicago Bears season|vaunted Chicago Bears]] defense in a 38–24 victory.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198512020mia.htm |title=Chicago Bears at Miami Dolphins – December 2nd, 1985 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=February 28, 2018}} The loss was the only one that the Bears experienced that season. Marino again led the league in completions, yards, and touchdown passes and was named 1st Team AP All-Pro.{{cite web|title=Dan Marino|url=http://www.miamidolphins.com/lockerroom/teamroster/teamroster_marino_d.asp|publisher=Miami Dolphins|access-date=February 10, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001203160800/http://www.miamidolphins.com/lockerroom/teamroster/teamroster_marino_d.asp|archive-date=December 3, 2000}}{{cite web|url=http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/member.aspx?PlayerId=238&tab=Highlights|title=Dan Marino: Highlights|publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame|access-date=February 10, 2015|archive-date=February 11, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150211095037/http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/member.aspx?PlayerId=238&tab=Highlights|url-status=dead}} On September 7, 1986, 8 days shy of his 25th birthday, Marino threw his 100th touchdown pass in a 50–28 loss to San Diego. Marino accomplished that feat in just 44 games – the fastest in NFL history. In the 1986 season, Marino threw for 4,746 yards and 44 touchdowns.{{cite web |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/danmarino/2501869/careerstats |title=Dan Marino Career Stats |publisher=National Football League |access-date=January 28, 2016}} Marino became the first QB in NFL history to record three consecutive seasons of 30 or more touchdown passes; 48 in 1984, 30 in 1985, and 44 in 1986. Marino again led the league in completions, yards and touchdown passes (the first and only QB in NFL history to lead in all three categories for three consecutive seasons). Marino was also named 1986 first team AP All-Pro, becoming the first and still only quarterback in NFL history to be named AP All-Pro in each of their first four seasons.{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} In 1987, Marino threw for 3,245 yards and 26 touchdowns in a strike-shortened 12 game season. Marino's 26 touchdown passes led the AFC, marking the fourth consecutive year that he led the conference in touchdown passes.{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Passing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/passing.htm |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} Marino was also named to the Pro Bowl, his fifth Pro Bowl selection in his five years in the league, becoming the first and still only quarterback in NFL history be elected to the Pro Bowl in each of their first five seasons. ===Mid-career=== In 1988, Marino threw for 4,434 yards and 28 touchdowns and was named NEA 2nd Team All-Pro despite the Dolphins finishing at 6–10.{{Cite web |title=Dan Marino 1988 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MariDa00/gamelog/1988/ |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} As a result of his 4,434 yards passing, Marino became the first quarterback in NFL history to throw for 4,000 or more yards in four different seasons. Marino had been tied with Dan Fouts for the most 4,000-yard passing seasons with three. Marino led the entire NFL in completions and passing yards and led the AFC in touchdown passes for a fifth consecutive year. No one else in history has led the AFC in touchdown passes for even three consecutive seasons, and only two ([[Peyton Manning]] and [[Patrick Mahomes]]) have done it back-to-back. [[File:USMC-05507 (cropped).jpg|thumb|200px|Marino in 1990]] In 1992, Marino again led the Dolphins to the AFC Championship game while passing for 4,116 yards and 24 touchdowns and was named 2nd Team NEA All-Pro [https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MariDa00.htm]. His 4,116 passing yards led the entire NFL and marked the fifth time in his NFL career that he led the league in passing yards. His 24 touchdown passes led the AFC for a record 6th time.{{Cite web |title=1992 NFL Passing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1992/passing.htm |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} In 1993, Miami was strongly favored at the start of the year to make it back to the AFC championship game and possibly the Super Bowl. However, after throwing a swing pass during a game in Cleveland, Marino, who was untouched on the play, crumpled to the ground in pain with a torn [[Achilles tendon]] and was out for the season. Marino later said, "I felt like I got kicked".{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Yk1TAAAAIBAJ&pg=1847,6044902&dq=dan+marino+achilles+tendon&hl=en|title=The Deseret News – Google News Archive Search|website=news.google.com}} Backup quarterback [[Scott Mitchell (quarterback)|Scott Mitchell]] had an impressive series of starts before suffering an injury of his own. [[Steve DeBerg]] started the last 4 games of the season. Mitchell signed a free-agent contract with the [[Detroit Lions]], and Miami signed veteran quarterback [[Bernie Kosar]] from the [[Dallas Cowboys]] as a backup. Wearing a special shoe on one foot, and having a right calf that was visibly atrophied, Marino was the starting quarterback at the opening of the 1994 season. In the [[1994 NFL season|1994 season]] opener, a home game versus the [[New England Patriots]] and quarterback [[Drew Bledsoe]], the two quarterbacks put up a combined 894 yards (Marino, 473 yards; Bledsoe, 421 yards) and nine passing touchdowns (Marino, 5; Bledsoe, 4), with Miami winning 39–35. Later in the season, Marino led a comeback win on the road against the New York Jets (28–24), a game famous for Marino's execution of a fake spike for the winning touchdown pass, a play known as "[[The Clock Play]]". The Dolphins finished 10–6 as Marino passed for 4,453 yards and 30 TD passes (which again led the AFC and extended his record to a 7th time), and he was named the NFL's Comeback Player of the Year by the [[Pro Football Writers Association]]. He was also named 2nd Team AP All-Pro. After missing the postseason in 1993, Miami came back to the playoffs in 1994.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/|title=Miami Dolphins Franchise Encyclopedia|publisher=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]|date=2017|access-date=April 5, 2017}} Placing third overall in the AFC, Miami was pitted against the Kansas City Chiefs in what became the final NFL game played by Montana.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199412310mia.htm|title=Wild Card – Kansas City Chiefs at Miami Dolphins – December 31st, 1994|publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=April 5, 2017}}{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/10056363/the_gettysburg_times/|agency=Associated Press|author=Steve Wilstein|page=16|title=Golden Boy says goodbye|date=April 19, 1995|newspaper=[[The Gettysburg Times]]|location=San Francisco, California|access-date=April 5, 2017|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{open access}} Marino threw 257 yards and two touchdown passes, contributing to Miami's 27–17 win. The Dolphins reached the AFC Divisional Playoff round, where they competed with the San Diego Chargers. Three touchdown passes by Marino in the first half allowed the Dolphins to lead 21–6, before the Chargers staged a comeback and took the lead toward the end of the fourth quarter. In the final moments of the game, Marino tried to set up a good position for a field goal, but with little time left at the Chargers' 30-yard line, [[Pete Stoyanovich]] was forced to attempt a 48-yard field goal. Stoyanovich missed, ending the game with a 22–21 loss for Miami.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199501080sdg.htm|title=Divisional Round – Miami Dolphins at San Diego Chargers – January 8th, 1995|publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=April 5, 2017}} Marino started in 14 out of 16 games in the 1995 season. He suffered a hip injury in week 6 against the Indianapolis Colts and was replaced by [[Bernie Kosar]] in the following two games. Throughout the regular season, Marino threw 3,668 yards and 24 touchdowns. Despite falling to 9–7 and to third place in the [[AFC East]], the Dolphins again advanced to the playoffs because they placed sixth in the AFC. In the wildcard round against the Buffalo Bills, Miami dominated in passing – with Marino passing 422 yards – while Buffalo was far ahead of Miami for rushing yards (341 yards). In terms of scoring, Buffalo held a wide lead throughout the game. The Dolphins remained scoreless until the fourth quarter, when they scored 22 points, which included two touchdown passes from Marino. However, Miami fell well short of a comeback and lost 37–22. Despite the Playoff disappointment, the 1995 season was a historic one for Marino as he set NFL career records for the most attempts, completions, passing yards, TD passes and 300-yard games. He was also named 2nd Team AP All-Pro. On November 10, 1996, against Indianapolis, Marino became the first quarterback in NFL history to throw for 50,000 career passing yards.{{cite web | last=Dorsey | first=Patrick | title=Yearbook, Nov. 10: Dan Marino hits 50,000 | website=ESPN.com | date=2012-11-10 | url=https://www.espn.com/blog/playbook/visuals/post/_/id/10061/yearbook-nov-10-dan-marino-hits-50000 | access-date=2026-04-06}} On November 29, 1998, against New Orleans, Marino threw for three touchdowns. [[File:2005 Dan Marino.jpg|thumb|right|Marino's bronze bust at the Pro Football Hall of Fame]] ===Legacy=== During Marino's career, the Dolphins were perennial playoff contenders, reaching the postseason in 10 of his 17 seasons. He was selected to play in nine Pro Bowls (1983–1987, 1991, 1992, 1994, 1995), seven times as a starter, but due to injuries he only played in two of the games (1984, 1992). He was named first- or second-team All-Pro eight times and earned All-AFC honors six times.{{Cite web |title=Dan Marino |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/dan-marino |access-date=2024-06-14 |website=Pro Football Hall of Fame |language=en}} Marino is the only QB in NFL History to have won all five major individual season awards: 1983 Rookie of the Year (The Sporting News), NFL MVP (1984); NFL Offensive Player of the Year (1984); NFL Comeback Player of the Year (1994); and NFL Man of the Year (1998), which recognizes charitable work off the field. Marino threw the most TD passes in the decade of the 1980s (220) and threw for the most passing yards in the decade of the 1990s (33,508). In 1999, Marino was ranked 27th on ''[[The Sporting News]]'' list of the 100 greatest football players, making him the highest-ranking Dolphins player.{{cite web|title=TSN 100 Greatest |work=sportingnews.com |url=http://archive.sportingnews.com/nfl/100/list-complete.html |access-date=July 14, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051105085403/http://archive.sportingnews.com/nfl/100/list-complete.html |archive-date=November 5, 2005 }} In 2010, he was ranked number 25 on the NFL's ''Top 100 Greatest Players'' list.[http://top100.nfl.com/all-time-100 "The Top 100: NFL's Greatest Players"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130730004815/http://top100.nfl.com/all-time-100 |date=July 30, 2013 }} NFL.com Marino was known for his quick release, and despite the fact that he was not skilled at scrambling, Marino possessed a natural awareness in the pocket, often sliding a step or two to avoid the pass rush.{{cite book|last =Sterngass|first =Jon|title =Dan Marino (Football Superstars)|publisher =Chelsea House Publications|year =2008|isbn =978-0-7910-9606-2|page =[https://archive.org/details/danmarino0000ster/page/62 62]|url-access =registration|url =https://archive.org/details/danmarino0000ster/page/62}} As of the conclusion of the [[2024 NFL season|2024 NFL regular season]], Marino's 155 wins rank eighth among [[most wins by a starting quarterback (NFL)|NFL quarterbacks]], behind [[Tom Brady]], [[Peyton Manning]], [[Brett Favre]], [[Drew Brees]], [[Aaron Rodgers]], [[Ben Roethlisberger]], and [[John Elway]]. In a year of accolades from the franchise he led for many years, the Dolphins also installed a life-size bronze statue of Marino at [[Pro Player Stadium]] (now Hard Rock Stadium) and renamed Stadium Street to Dan Marino Boulevard.{{Cite web |last=Bouchette |first=Ed |date=February 6, 2005 |title=Marino Interview |url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/05037/453536.stm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929211647/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/05037/453536.stm |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 29, 2007 |access-date=July 14, 2007 |website=post-gazette.com}} In 2003, Marino was honored for his outstanding NCAA career at [[University of Pittsburgh|Pitt]] with an induction into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]]. In early 2004, Marino briefly returned to the [[Miami Dolphins]] as Senior Vice President of Football Operations but resigned from the newly created position only three weeks later, saying the role was not in the best interest of either his family or the Dolphin organization. Marino was elected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2005, one of only five Dolphins to be elected in their first year of eligibility ([[Paul Warfield]], [[Jim Langer]], [[Don Shula]] and [[Jason Taylor (American football)|Jason Taylor]]). He was inducted into the Hall of Fame on August 7, 2005 and was introduced by his oldest son, Daniel. During his induction speech, Dan threw "one last pass" to former teammate [[Mark Clayton (American football, born 1961)|Mark Clayton]], who was sitting in the audience. Marino served as an analyst for [[CBS Sports|CBS]]'s Sunday pregame show ''[[The NFL Today]]'' from 2002 to 2013. On February 18, 2014, it was announced that Marino, along with [[Shannon Sharpe]] were being [[dismissal (employment)|relieved of their duties]] as on-air commentators on ''The NFL Today'' and were being replaced by [[Tony Gonzalez]] and [[Bart Scott]].{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=Nate |date=February 18, 2014 |title=CBS hires Tony Gonzalez, parts with two Hall-of-Fame analysts |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2014/02/18/cbs-tony-gonzalez-shannon-sharpe-dan-marino/5580021/ |access-date=February 18, 2014 |website=USA Today}} He was formerly a studio analyst on [[Home Box Office|HBO]]'s ''[[Inside the NFL]]'', from 2002 to 2007. On August 24, 2014, Marino announced he would return to the Dolphins as a special adviser.{{Cite web |date=August 24, 2014 |title=Dan Marino accepts job with Dolphins |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/11401299/dan-marino-accepts-role-miami-dolphins-front-office |access-date=August 24, 2014 |website=[[ESPN.com]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]}} Former Miami Dolphins quarterback [[Tua Tagovailoa]] revealed that Marino regularly attends Dolphins quarterback meetings to give his opinion and input on how to be a better quarterback.{{Cite web |last=Papke |first=Grey |date=2021-08-25 |title=Hall of Famer Dan Marino helping out in Dolphins QB meetings |url=https://larrybrownsports.com/football/tua-tagovailoa-dan-marino-dolphins-qb-meetings/583054 |access-date=2024-06-14 |website=Larry Brown Sports |language=en}} ==Life outside football== ===Ownership in NASCAR=== [[File:FirstPlusDanMarino13JerryNadeau.jpg|thumb|left|267px|Marino's #13 NASCAR racecar]] In 1997, Marino became involved in a marketing role with [[Cheever Racing|Team Cheever]] of the [[Indy Racing League]] through FirstPlus Mortgage, the sponsor of the car. In 1998, Marino co-owned a [[NASCAR]] [[Winston Cup Series]] racing team with driver [[Bill Elliott]], creating Elliott-Marino Motorsports.{{cite web|last=Pockrass |first=Bob |url=http://www.sportingnews.com/nascar/story/2013-01-31/super-bowl-2013-nfl-dan-marino-randy-moss-brett-favre-troy-aikman-joe-gibbs |title=NFL and NASCAR: Former NFL stars who dabbled in stock-car racing |work=[[Sporting News]] |date=January 31, 2014 |access-date=March 2, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130522121301/http://www.sportingnews.com/nascar/story/2013-01-31/super-bowl-2013-nfl-dan-marino-randy-moss-brett-favre-troy-aikman-joe-gibbs |archive-date=May 22, 2013 }} The team's car number was #13, Marino's uniform number, and had primary sponsorship from FirstPlus Mortgage, whose company colors, coincidentally, were turquoise, orange, and white – similar to aqua and coral, the team colors of the Miami Dolphins. The team chose rookie driver [[Jerry Nadeau]] to pilot the car at the start of the season; he was later released and the team went through a rotation of drivers. The team failed to qualify for several races, but did post a top-5 finish at [[Phoenix International Raceway]] late in the season with [[Ted Musgrave]] driving. The team only lasted the 1998 season and closed afterward. ===Dan Marino Foundation=== The Dan Marino Foundation was established in 1992 by Marino and his wife, Claire, after their son, Michael, was diagnosed with [[autism]].{{cite web|title=Dan the Man |work=nba.com |url=http://www.nba.com/heat/news/dan_the_man_051107.html |access-date=July 14, 2007}} The foundation has distributed over $22 million to research, services, and treatment programs serving children with neurodevelopment disabilities. The Dan Marino Center, which opened in 1995 along with the Miami Children's Hospital, is an integrated neurodevelopmental center specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of children at risk for developmental and psychological problems. The center saw more than 48,000 children last year alone. Marino has teamed with other celebrities to raise awareness about [[autistic spectrum disorder]]s, including fellow NFL quarterback [[Doug Flutie]], whose son also has an autism diagnosis. On November 7, 2005, the [[National Basketball Association]]'s [[Miami Heat]] honored Marino's charitable works and recognized his service to [[South Florida]] with a halftime tribute, as well as a large donation to the Marino Foundation. Though a Heat jersey with his name and #13 was unveiled, this did not constitute retirement of his number by the Heat, and is currently worn by Heat big man [[Bam Adebayo]]. On March 23, 2010, The Dan Marino Foundation held its first "Walk about Autism". Over 6000 walkers participated, as well as 420 volunteers provided by the Miami Dolphins Special Teams. The money raised benefited several funds including the Autism Societies of Miami-Dade and Broward; the University of Miami-[[Nova Southeastern University]] Center for Autism and Related Disabilities; the Florida Atlantic University Center for Autism and Related Disabilities; and the Dan Marino Foundation. ===In popular culture=== [[File:Super Bowl XLI pre-game show in Miami.jpg|thumb|250px|Marino with [[Shannon Sharpe]], two [[United States Air Force]] members, and [[Boomer Esiason]] during the [[Super Bowl XLI]] pre-game show in Miami]] Marino acted in the 1994 comedy ''[[Ace Ventura: Pet Detective]]'' alongside [[Jim Carrey]] and [[Courteney Cox]] where he played himself.{{cite web |last=Zaksheske |first=Dan |date=2024-02-07 |title=Dan Marino Jokingly Takes Credit For Jim Carrey's Success Thanks To Ace Ventura Role |url=https://www.outkick.com/sports/dan-marino-jim-carrey-success-ace-ventura-pet-detective |access-date=2026-04-06 |publisher=OutKick}} Marino made a cameo appearance in the [[Adam Sandler]] film ''[[Little Nicky]]'' wherein he asked [[Satan]] for a [[Super Bowl ring]].{{cite web | last=Hough | first=Quinn | title=Little Nicky Cast: Every Cameo In The Adam Sandler Movie | website=ScreenRant | date=2020-12-05 | url=https://screenrant.com/little-nicky-movie-cast-character-cameos-guide/ | access-date=2026-04-06}} In 1999, he voiced himself in a guest-starring role in ''[[The Simpsons]]'' Season ten episode "[[Sunday, Cruddy Sunday]]".{{cite web | title=The Simpsons S10E12 "Sunday, Cruddy Sunday" | website=TV Tropes | date=2013-05-10 | url=https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/TheSimpsonsS10E12SundayCruddySunday | access-date=2026-04-06}} Marino also had cameo roles in ''[[Holy Man]]'' and ''[[Bad Boys II]]''. The couple have six children together.{{cite news|title=Miami QB Marino takes bride|date=January 31, 1985|newspaper=The Oregonian|page=E7}} Through his sister Cindi, Marino is brother-in-law to longtime [[KDKA (AM)|KDKA radio]] personality Larry Richert, who currently serves as the announcer for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] at [[Acrisure Stadium]] in addition to his radio duties and was once a [[meteorologist]] for [[KDKA-TV]] when the radio & TV stations were both owned by [[Westinghouse Broadcasting|Group W]].{{cite web | last=Rutkoski | first=Rex | title=Everyone knows KDKA morning radio host Larry Richert | website=TribLIVE.com | date=2012-07-13 | url=https://archive.triblive.com/aande/more-a-and-e/everyone-knows-kdka-morning-radio-host-larry-richert/ | access-date=2026-04-06}} Along with former [[WDVE]] personality [[Jim Krenn]], Marino and Richert co-own [[Yinzer]] Dogs, a [[hot dog stand]] that started off as a [[food truck]] before opening a permanent location in suburban [[Cranberry Township, Butler County, Pennsylvania|Cranberry Township]] with plans to open a second location in the [[Strip District (Pittsburgh)|Strip District]] before the [[2026 NFL draft]] scheduled to take place in Pittsburgh.{{cite web |last=Dabkowski |first=Jake |date=2025-06-12 |title=Backed by local celebrities, Yinzer Dogs set to open first brick-and-mortar location in Cranberry |url=https://www.wpxi.com/news/local/backed-by-local-celebrities-yinzer-dogs-set-open-first-brick-and-mortar-location-cranberry/TYLPAYJQGRAXBJSEY7UGCGVGHI/ |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=WPXI}} Marino was awarded an honorary doctorate degree in broadcast journalism by his alma mater, the [[University of Pittsburgh]], in 2005. He delivered the commencement speech at the university's 2008 graduation ceremony.{{Cite web |date=April 27, 2008 |title=Marino Tells Graduates to "Go After Your Passion," "Nurture Your Relationships," "Touch Someone's Life in a Positive Way" |url=https://www.news.pitt.edu/news/marino-tells-graduates-go-after-your-passion-nurture-your-relationships-touch-someones-life-pos |access-date=2024-06-14 |website=Pitt.edu}} In January 2013, Marino admitted to fathering a child with CBS employee Donna Savattere in 2005, a fact he only shared with his wife.
